$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
f_1(t)=t,\qquad f_2(t)=t^2+1, \qquad h(t)= 5t^3,

in the vector space $V = \mathcal{C}[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1],$ where the inner product is defined as

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^1 x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

Let's find the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto the subspace

$$
S= \textrm{Span}\{f_1(t), f_2(t)\},
$$

 

given that $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to this inner product. 

Since the set $\{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,h(t) 
= \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,h(t) + \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,h(t).
$$

Let's now compute these projections:

- First, we compute  the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_1(t)\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,h(t) & =\frac{⟨h(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot t \\  & =3t\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we compute  the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_2(t)\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,h(t) & =\frac{⟨h(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{2}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Note: We used the fact that the integrand in the numerator is an odd function, so its integral over $[-1,1]$ must be zero.

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,h(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,h(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,h(t) \\  & =3t+0 \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "975c7894-a67f-5528-875e-2e55a94d99b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6130 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} {:course/id
